Trong tiếng Việt, âm cuối như “t, c, p”: In English, final consonants carry grammatical and lexical distinctions: “rice” differs from “rise”, and “life” from “live”. Say final stops /p, t, k/ clearly (a light release is fine; do not drop them), keep /s/ sharp, and make sure /z/ has clear vocal cord vibration. Vowels are also noticeably longer before voiced consonants (/b, d, ɡ, z, v/) than before voiceless ones.
Thần chú: “Âm cuối là nửa nghĩa của từ.”: Tip: Final consonants carry much of a word’s meaning, so do not drop them. Record yourself and replay only the ends of words; if you cannot hear them, a listener cannot either. Then link them into the next vowel (“fact is”, “price of”).
Cách đọc -ed phụ thuộc vào ÂM cuối của đ: The pronunciation of the regular -ed suffix depends entirely on the final sound of the root verb. Only when the base verb ends in the sounds /t/ or /d/ does -ed add an extra syllable /ɪd/. Otherwise, it is an attached single consonant: /t/ after voiceless sounds, and /d/ after voiced sounds and vowels.
Câu thần chú: “Tiền Đô → /ɪd/” (t, d thê: Tip: “T and D add a beat” – /ɪd/ appears only after /t/ or /d/. Otherwise touch your throat: voiced /d/ vibrates, voiceless /t/ does not. A few adjectives (naked, wicked, learned, aged) take /ɪd/.
Đuôi -s/-es xuất hiện ở danh từ số nhiều: The third-person singular, plural and possessive -s/-es endings mirror the -ed rule. After sibilants (/s, z, ʃ, ʒ, tʃ, dʒ/) an extra syllable /ɪz/ is added. After voiceless consonants it sounds as /s/; after voiced consonants and vowels it becomes /z/.
Mẹo: -s là “tấm gương” của -ed. Âm vô th: Tip: Sibilants need /ɪz/ to stay distinct. After vowels and voiced consonants let the vocal cords buzz for /z/ (“days” /deɪz/, “plans” /plænz/); after voiceless consonants use /s/. Watch the irregular “says” /sez/ and “does” /dʌz/.
Cả /θ/ và /ð/ đều là âm “giữa hai răng”:: English dental fricatives /θ/ (voiceless: think, three) and /ð/ (voiced: this, weather) are produced by resting the tip of the tongue gently between the front teeth (or behind the upper incisors) and pushing a continuous airstream through the constriction without stopping. Unlike Vietnamese “th”, which is an aspirated stop, they are fricatives: the air keeps flowing.
Thần chú: “Lè lưỡi – thổi hơi.” Nếu khôn: Tip: Put the tongue tip lightly between the teeth and let the air flow. If the sound stops like a click, you are saying /t/ or /d/ instead of /θ/ or /ð/.
/s/: đầu lưỡi gần lợi trên, môi dẹt, tiế: /s/ and /z/ are alveolar: the tongue tip is close to the ridge behind the upper teeth, the lips are spread, and the sound is thin and sharp. /ʃ/ and /ʒ/ are post-alveolar: the tongue pulls back a little and the lips round and protrude, giving a darker “shh”. /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ are affricates: a full stop of air released into /ʃ/ or /ʒ/ (chair, job). All four sounds /ʃ ʒ tʃ dʒ/ are normally made with some lip rounding; /ʒ/ is voiced and mostly occurs in the middle of words (decision, usually).
Tip: Four rounded-lip sounds: /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /tʃ/, /dʒ/. Lip rounding is an easy cue, but the main difference from /s/ and /z/ is that the tongue pulls back.
/n/ là âm mũi: hơi đi ra đằng mũi (bịt m: /n/ is a nasal: air flows through the nose (pinch your nose and it is blocked). /l/ is a lateral: the tongue tip touches the ridge and air passes along the sides, with no nasal airflow. At the end of a word (school, feel) /l/ is “dark”: the back of the tongue rises, giving a soft “w”-like quality, but it must not be dropped. Consonant clusters such as /str/, /spl/, /kts/ and /sts/ are said in one continuous breath, without inserting a schwa between the consonants.
Thần chú: “Một hơi, không ơ.” Một cụm ph: Tip: One breath, no extra vowel. Say a cluster as a single block: the “str” in “street” has no vowel inside it.
Mỗi từ nhiều âm tiết có một âm tiết được: In English, stressed syllables are usually longer, louder and higher in pitch, while unstressed syllables often reduce to /ə/ or /ɪ/. Wrong stress can hinder recognition more than a wrong single sound. In IPA the mark ˈ comes before the stressed syllable. Several patterns are useful tendencies, not exceptionless rules: two-syllable nouns and adjectives are often stressed on the first syllable, two-syllable verbs on the second, and suffixes such as -tion, -ic and -ity usually pull the stress onto the syllable just before them.
Thần chú: “Danh trước – Động sau – Đuôi: Tip: Nouns first, verbs second, and stress the syllable before endings like -tion, -ic and -ity. These are strong tendencies with exceptions, so check the dictionary for new words.
Khi thêm hậu tố, trọng âm có thể di chuy: When a suffix is added, stress often moves to a different syllable, and the vowel of the previously stressed syllable reduces: the first “o” of photograph is /əʊ/, becomes /ə/ in photography, and is /əʊ/ again in photographic (/ˈfəʊtəɡrɑːf/ → /fəˈtɒɡrəfi/ → /ˌfəʊtəˈɡræfɪk/). Keeping the stress of the base word (PHOtography) is an error that listeners notice easily.
Mẹo: Đếm từ cuối lên. -y/-ity: thường nh: Tip: Count back from the end. -y/-ity usually put the stress on the third syllable from the end (phoˈtography, eˈconomy); -ic/-tion/-sion/-cian put it on the syllable just before the ending (photoˈgraphic, poliˈtician). Suffixes such as -ism usually leave the stress where it was (criticize → criticism), with exceptions such as Catholic → Catholicism.
Tiếng Anh có nhịp dựa trên trọng âm: các: In natural spoken English, content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs), negatives and question words receive sentence stress, while grammatical function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns, conjunctions) are often reduced to weak forms with /ə/ in the middle of a sentence. Stressed words tend to fall at fairly regular intervals, so weak words are squeezed between them. Function words keep strong forms at the end of a clause, when stressed for contrast, and negatives such as can’t are separate words with a full vowel (UK /kɑːnt/, US /kænt/). Saying every word with a full vowel makes speech sound stiff and robotic.
Thần chú: “Nội dung thì nhấn – chức năng: Tip: Stress the content, glide over the grammar. Positive “can” is usually /kən/, whereas “can’t” keeps a full vowel: /kɑːnt/ in British English, /kænt/ in American English.
Ngữ điệu là sự lên xuống cao độ của cả c: Intonation is the rise and fall of pitch across a phrase, concentrated on the nucleus, the most prominent word of the thought group. Vietnamese uses tones on single syllables to change word meaning; English uses intonation over whole phrases to signal attitude, grammatical structure and intent. A fall usually signals that the information is complete (statements, Wh-questions); a rise typically marks yes/no questions and checking (“Do you like it? ↗”, “Really? ↗”), although British speakers also often fall on yes/no questions; a fall-rise signals reservation or that there is more to come.
Mẹo: “Xong thì xuống, hỏi có/không thì l: Tip: “Finished, fall; yes/no question, rise; more to come, hang.” A wider pitch range also makes you sound more engaged and natural.
Người bản ngữ không nói từng từ tách rời: Fluent speech links words instead of pronouncing isolated tokens. Main features: consonant-to-vowel linking (turn off), /j/ and /w/ glides between vowels (the‿/j/‿end, go‿/w/‿out), linking /r/ in British accents (far‿away), elision of /t, d/ between consonants (next door), and assimilation, where a sound changes under the influence of its neighbour (ten people, did you).
Mẹo: “Phụ âm đi tìm nguyên âm.” Mỗi khi: Tip: Consonants look for vowels. Attach a final consonant to the next word if it starts with a vowel: “an‿apple” sounds like “a napple”.
Người nói tự nhiên chia câu thành các “c: Divide speech into meaningful thought groups (tone units) of roughly 3–7 words, separated by brief pauses. Each chunk carries one central nucleus. Break at clause boundaries; avoid breaking between an article and its noun or a preposition and its object, which makes you sound as if you are searching for words. Steady rhythm with purposeful pauses sounds more fluent than speed.
Thần chú: “Một hơi – một ý – một điểm nh: Tip: One breath, one idea, one nucleus. Good fluency is not maximum speed but steady rhythm with purposeful pauses.
Giọng Anh chuẩn (RP) không đọc r ở cuối: RP and other non-rhotic British accents do not pronounce a final r, yet two opposite phenomena are worth recognising. Linking /r/: a written final “r” is pronounced when the next word begins with a vowel (far away). Intrusive /r/: after /ə/, /ɑː/ and /ɔː/ there is no “r” in the spelling, yet speakers add /r/ before a following vowel: “criteria are” /kraɪˈtɪəriər ə/, “law and order” /ˌlɔːr ən ˈɔːdə/. It also occurs inside derived words: “drawing” is often /ˈdrɔːrɪŋ/ and “withdrawal” /wɪðˈdrɔːrəl/. Some speakers regard intrusive /r/ as non-standard and avoid it, so you only need to recognise it. Standard American English pronounces final r and does not need it (a few accents, such as Boston, do have it).
Mẹo: Nếu bạn nghe thấy /r/ mà chính tả k: Tip: If you hear an /r/ that the spelling does not have, it is an intrusive /r/: in British accents it appears only after /ə/, /ɑː/ or /ɔː/, before a vowel.
Trong bài này, CHỮ HOA là từ mang nhân (: In this lesson CAPITALS mark the word that carries the nucleus (lexical stress inside words is not marked). Each thought group has one nucleus, the word that carries the main pitch movement. By default it falls on the last content word. Speakers move it to mark information structure: new information is stressed and given information (already mentioned) is de-accented, and contrast or correction pulls the nucleus onto the word that differs. The same sentence changes meaning when the focus moves: “I didn’t say HE took it” (perhaps someone else did) versus “I didn’t say he TOOK it” (perhaps he borrowed it).
Mẹo: Hỏi trước khi nói: “Thông tin nào l: Tip: Ask yourself which piece of information is new to the listener, put the nucleus on it, and lower the pitch on what they already know.
Ở trình độ C1, người nói điều khiển ngữ: At C1, speakers steer intonation across clauses. When a subordinate clause comes first (Although…, When…, If…), the last stressed word of that clause often carries a rise or a fall-rise (↘↗), signalling that the sentence is not finished; the main clause that follows usually ends with a fall (↘), signalling completion. These are tendencies, not fixed rules. The fall-rise also conveys reservation or that there is more to say; it is not a marker of conditionality.
Mẹo: Xem mệnh đề phụ như chiếc cầu treo:: Tip: Treat a leading subordinate clause like an open phrase: keep the pitch suspended or rising at its end so the listener expects the main clause.
Dạng yếu nâng cao: should have, would ha: Advanced Weak Forms: should have, would have…
Ở tốc độ nói tự nhiên, các cấu trúc “khu: In connected speech, perfect modals such as should have, would have, could have and must have are usually reduced when unstressed: the modal vowel weakens to /ə/ and have becomes /əv/, giving /ʃəd əv/, /wəd əv/, /kəd əv/ and /məst əv/. The spelled contractions should’ve, would’ve and so on sound almost the same. Because /əv/ sounds like “of”, many writers produce the error “could of”. The modal returns to its strong form under contrastive stress (“I COULD have gone” /kʊd/), and have keeps its strong form at the end of a clause (“Yes, you should have!” /hæv/).
Thần chú: “Trợ từ là bóng râm, động từ c: Tip: Keep auxiliaries in the shadow: glide through the modal chain and save the stress for the main verb.
Tiếng Việt thường được mô tả là nhịp the: Vietnamese is usually described as syllable-timed, with syllables of similar length. English leans towards stress-timing: stressed syllables tend to come at fairly regular intervals however many unstressed syllables fall between them. “CATS CHASE MICE”, “The CATS are CHASing the MICE” and “The CATS have been CHASing the MICE” all have three beats; the longer sentences are not twice as long, because the weak syllables are squeezed and reduced. Measurements show this is a perceptual tendency, not a metronome. Understanding it helps you stop delivering every word with equal weight.
Mẹo: Hình dung trọng âm là những bước ch: Tip: Think of stressed syllables as steady footsteps: whether one or three small words fall between two steps, the steps keep landing at fairly even intervals.
Câu hỏi đuôi (question tag) có hai ngữ đ: Question tags commonly take one of two intonation patterns with different meanings. A falling tone (↘) on the tag usually means the speaker is fairly sure and invites agreement: “It’s a rather ambitious target, isn’t it? ↘”. A rising tone (↗) usually means a real question: “You haven’t had a chance to review the draft yet, have you? ↗”. Tags such as “right?” and the suggestion “shall we?” often rise as well, because they invite a response. These are tendencies; context and attitude still decide.
Mẹo: “Biết rồi thì xuống, chưa biết thì: Tip: Down when you already know, up when you really don't. To invite a nod of agreement, let the pitch fall on the tag.
